clue.text: Box opened by wizard with bishop's long key

indicators.note: opening a thing makes a gap in it, so what follows is planted inside the word rather than parked next to it

parts.note: to box is to spar, trading punches in a gym
a wizard at something is an ace at it, an expert
B is the bishop in chess notation

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'Box' as a container a wizard opens; it is the verb, to fight. Chess supplies the B and the expert supplies the ACE, both worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: The space bar is the long horizontal key across the bottom of a keyboard, the only one struck with a thumb.

clue.text: Italian's first proper answer

parts.note: prim means proper in the starchy, disapproving sense
A is the standard short form of answer, as on a quiz sheet

explanation.walkthrough: 'Italian's first' looks like an instruction to take the opening letter of Italian; it is asking for the Italian word for first instead.
explanation.definitionFit: Prima is the Italian feminine word meaning first, familiar in English from prima donna and prima ballerina.

clue.text: E.g. Calvin and Hobbes love getting into wagon and going

parts.note: a cart is the horse-drawn wagon

indicators.note: getting into a vehicle means climbing inside it, so the letter lands within the word rather than beside it

parts.note: a machine that is going is on
love is nil in tennis, written as the round nought

explanation.walkthrough: Love for O comes from tennis scoring and turns up everywhere. The surface reads as a child's day out, which is what hides the fact that two of its words are a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Calvin and Hobbes is Bill Watterson's newspaper strip about a boy and his tiger, so the clue defines by naming one example.

clue.text: Charming parent stuck with Aunt Ethel every so often

indicators.note: being stuck with something means it is lodged in the middle of what you already have, not tacked on the end

parts.note: to bring up a child is to parent them

indicators.note: every so often means at intervals rather than continuously, so only every second letter is taken

parts.note: counting through the two names and keeping the second letter of each pair yields four

explanation.walkthrough: 'Parent' is the verb here, the thing you do to a child rather than the person doing it, and that shift is what keeps the long phrase out of sight.
explanation.definitionFit: Buttering someone up is flattering them to get something out of them, which is charming in its manipulative sense.

clue.text: One could be cavalryman crossing area's frontier

definitions.text: One could be cavalryman crossing area's frontier

indicators.note: one thing crossing another passes through it, so the letter goes inside rather than alongside

parts.note: a cavalryman fights on horseback, so he is a rider

indicators.note: a frontier is the edge you meet first, so it points at the opening letter of the word before it

parts.note: the leading letter of area, its border on the page

explanation.walkthrough: Every word does double duty: the same sentence that pictures a horseman slipping over a border is also the instruction that builds him.
explanation.definitionFit: The whole clue reads straight, since someone crossing a border to strike and run is exactly what the word names.

clue.text: Lip turned grey — effect of heat, you see

indicators.note: a thing turned round faces the other way, so its letters are read starting from the back

parts.note: the lip of a cup is its rim, spun round here
to grey is to age, hair being the classic sign

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a face losing its colour, which is why 'grey' reads as an adjective. It is the verb, and nothing before the dash is about heat at all.
explanation.definitionFit: A mirage is the shimmering pool that appears on a hot road and is not there, heat playing tricks on the eye.

clue.text: Police came to rally

definitions.meaning: London's Metropolitan force, known everywhere by its short name
people who came together for a gathering assembled there

explanation.walkthrough: Three words, no joinery, and the seam falls after the first one. The surface pretends to report a demonstration being policed.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the London force everyone shortens; the other is the past tense of coming together, which is what a rally is.

clue.text: We learn in a forced way, repetition

indicators.note: forcing something bends it out of its natural shape, and letters bent out of shape come out in a different order

parts.note: seven letters of fodder, straight from the opening two words

explanation.walkthrough: The surface sounds like a grumble about rote schooling, so the last word reads as part of that complaint rather than as the definition sitting at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: A renewal is doing the same thing over again, the way renewing a lease or a vow repeats what was done before.

clue.text: Prisoner charges grand less than original charge for weapons

parts.note: G is the short form of a grand, a thousand pounds

indicators.note: to charge is to rush headlong at something, and a piece that rushes at a word ends up in the middle of it

parts.note: less than a figure is under it
a prisoner of war is a POW

explanation.walkthrough: 'Charges' looks like part of the definition, since a charge is what a weapon takes, and it is the instruction instead.
explanation.definitionFit: It was the original propellant charge packed behind the shot in muskets and cannon, long before smokeless powders arrived.

clue.text: Half of Stilgoe's Bitter ordered for Tim Rice?

indicators.note: half of a name keeps one part and throws the rest away, and here the front four letters are the survivors
drinks are ordered at a bar, but things put in order are arranged, and an arrangement can leave letters in a sequence they did not start in

parts.note: Richard Stilgoe is the British lyricist, and only his front half is wanted
bitter is the English ale, and all six of its letters go into the mix

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a drinks round at the theatre bar, and the two lyricists in it are doing different jobs: one supplies letters, the other is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Tim Rice wrote the words for Evita and Jesus Christ Superstar, so he is one example of the person who writes a show's text.

clue.text: Sister reported an absence

indicators.note: something reported is passed on by word of mouth, so you write down what the word sounds like rather than how it was spelt

parts.note: a sister in a convent is a nun, and the two words are said the same way

explanation.walkthrough: 'Sister' reads as a sibling until you say it out loud; the religious one is the sister the clue means, and the whole mechanism is in the sound.
explanation.definitionFit: It means not any at all, so it names the absence of a thing rather than any quantity of it.

clue.text: Leaflets now distributed round work all together

indicators.note: leaflets distributed are scattered in every direction, and scattered letters land somewhere other than where they started

parts.note: eleven letters of fodder from the pamphlets and the moment
a round shape is written as the letter O
op is short for opus, a composer's work

explanation.walkthrough: The trap is reading 'round' as an instruction to enclose something; here it is simply the round letter joining the fodder. Macduff gave the language the phrase, over his murdered family.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase means everything happening in one sudden action, all of it at once rather than piece by piece.

clue.text: Big spender delays start of ambitious moon shot

indicators.note: nerves or springs described as shot are wrecked, and a wrecked word no longer holds its letters in their proper order

parts.note: six letters of fodder, from the hold-ups on the launch pad

indicators.note: the start of a word is its opening letter, and only that one letter is taken

parts.note: the opening letter of ambitious joins the mix
four more letters, straight from the night sky

explanation.walkthrough: Comedian Harry Enfield's plasterer waved his wad at the camera in 1988 and handed British English a word for a flashy spender. The rocket surface hides him completely.
explanation.definitionFit: Loadsamoney, Harry Enfield's cash-waving character, became the British word for somebody who flaunts money and spends it freely.

clue.text: Frank's a hundred, with evidence to prove it

parts.note: C is the Roman numeral for a hundred
the joining word is spelled out as the conjunction itself
the card you produce to prove who you are is your ID

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a man named Frank turning a hundred with the birth certificate to show for it. Both scraps of wordplay are conventions worth banking.
explanation.definitionFit: Both words describe someone who says what they think without softening it, the plainest kind of honesty.

clue.text: Exit from garden behind shed I slam

indicators.note: behind means at the back, so the piece named before it ends up at the end of the build

parts.note: a snake sheds its skin by casting it off
the letter is taken at face value
the way out of a walled garden is its gate

explanation.walkthrough: 'Shed' is the verb, to cast off, and not the hut at the bottom of the garden, and that swap is the whole trick of the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: To castigate is to attack somebody in words, which is what a critic does when they slam a play.

clue.text: Woman on the street delighted to fit into parking space

indicators.note: fitting into a space means going inside it, so one word is planted within the other

parts.note: a marked space for one car is a bay
glad is plain delighted

explanation.walkthrough: A parking bay is the painted rectangle you reverse into, and the surface is somebody thrilled to squeeze the car in.
explanation.definitionFit: A bag lady is a homeless woman living on the street with everything she owns in carrier bags.

clue.text: Temper made Gauss add brackets the wrong way

indicators.note: to bracket a thing is to stand on both sides of it, which is what these words do to the letters between them
the run of letters sits in the clue pointing the opposite way to the grid, so it has to be read back

parts.note: seven letters in a row, running across the joins of these three words

explanation.walkthrough: The mathematician is there to make 'add' look like arithmetic. Nothing is being calculated: the letters are simply lying in the sentence, facing the wrong way.
explanation.definitionFit: To assuage grief is to soften it, and temper as a verb means exactly that, to moderate something harsh.

clue.text: Many men up there in trouble without her

indicators.note: something in trouble has been thrown into disarray, and letters in disarray no longer sit in their proper order
without means lacking, so the three letters that spell her are taken out of the word beside it

parts.note: five letters of fodder, taken as they stand
HER comes out of THERE and two letters survive

explanation.walkthrough: This entry runs down the grid, so 'up' looks like an instruction to reverse something. It lifts nothing here; it is just two more letters to shuffle.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the joke number for an indefinitely large amount, meaning many with nobody prepared to count them.

clue.text: Groom heartlessly pinched gold rings

indicators.note: to do a thing heartlessly is to do it with no heart, so the word loses the letter at its centre
a ring goes right round the outside of something, so these letters close around what is left

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry, the tincture on a coat of arms
to pinch is to steal, and STOLE has lost the letter at its heart

explanation.walkthrough: 'Groom' points at the stable rather than a wedding, and heraldic OR for gold is one of the conventions crosswords lean on hardest.
explanation.definitionFit: An ostler was the inn servant who looked after travellers' horses, which is what a groom does in a stable.

clue.text: Liberal America curtailed president's five year term

indicators.note: to curtail is to cut short, so the name gives up the letter standing at its end

parts.note: L is the ballot-paper abbreviation for Liberal
the United States, shortened as ever
Trump is the president, with his final letter docked

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is all politics, and the definition is Roman: an American president's term runs four years, not five, which is the wrong scent the clue lays.
explanation.definitionFit: A lustrum is the Roman span of five years, originally the gap between one census purification ceremony and the next.

clue.text: Queen wearing corset gets out of control

indicators.note: somebody wearing a garment is inside it, so the letter goes within the word beside it

parts.note: stays is the old word for a corset, stiffened with whalebone
R is Regina, the Latin queen a monarch signs herself

explanation.walkthrough: R for Regina is the crossword's standard queen, and stays for a corset is worth banking too, since Victorian underwear turns up in grids far more than in shops.
explanation.definitionFit: A dog or a thought that strays wanders off from where it is supposed to be, which is what getting out of control looks like.

clue.text: Weed in cool river tickles bathers on the bottom

parts.note: hip is cool in the slang sense, fashionable and in the know

indicators.note: in plants one word inside another rather than beside it, so the first piece lands part-way through the rest

parts.note: pot is the common slang for cannabis
the Po is the long river across northern Italy, a crossword regular
to tickle somebody is to amuse them, as in tickled pink

explanation.walkthrough: Four separate pieces hide inside one smooth riverbank picture, and the definition is the whimsical half: the setter is describing what is standing on the riverbed.
explanation.definitionFit: They spend their days submerged in African rivers, walking along the bottom, so they really are the bathers down there.

clue.text: Boiling apparatus not bubbling yet

definitions.meaning: the copper vessel in which a wash is boiled to make whisky
water sold without gas is flat, and the same word also means even now

explanation.walkthrough: Three senses, one word, and the whole clue reads as a single picture of a pot that has not come to the boil, which is what does the hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense is the apparatus that makes spirits; the other covers a drink with no bubbles and, as an adverb, yet.

clue.text: Composer who wanted quiet shut up

definitions.meaning: the American whose 4'33" is four and a half minutes of players not playing
to shut an animal up is to put it behind bars

explanation.walkthrough: The definition by example is the harder half: you need the composer whose most famous piece is silence, and then the everyday verb sitting beside him.
explanation.definitionFit: John Cage wrote 4'33", a piece of pure silence; and to cage an animal is to shut it up behind bars.

clue.text: Loss of brightness, with black day between spells of bad weather

indicators.note: between puts the letter in the gap, with one of the wet spells on either side of it

parts.note: B is black on a pencil and in chess
a spell of bad weather is a spell of rain
d is the standard short form of day in a date
the plural says there are two such spells, one on each side

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a weather forecast and the answer is about emigration. 'Spells' is the word doing the quiet work, since it has to be read as two of them.
explanation.definitionFit: A brain drain is a country losing its cleverest people to better jobs abroad, its brightness draining away.

clue.text: Club spa where Henry has gone

indicators.note: the phrase marks a letter as absent, asking what is left of the town once that symbol has departed

parts.note: the Somerset city of Bath, built on Roman hot springs, is England's spa town
the henry is the unit of inductance and its symbol is the single letter H

explanation.walkthrough: Two facts have to be held at once: the West Country spa city the Romans built, and the electrical unit named after Joseph Henry.
explanation.definitionFit: A bat is a shaped wooden club for striking a ball, so club names it by its blunt-instrument sense.

clue.text: One contributing to very little?

parts.note: the surface offers a person chipping in their small share of something
a derisory wage is always talked about in the plural, and the clue asks for a single one of them

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to unpick: the whole sentence is the definition. The move is spotting that the plural slang phrase for a trivial sum can be cut down to one of them.
explanation.definitionFit: Wages worth almost nothing are called peanuts, so a single one of them is what contributes to that sum.

clue.text: Vegan option really kind hosts left for Yolanda in the morning

indicators.note: for signals a swap, with whatever follows taking the place of the letter named before it
a host takes guests inside, so the surrounding letters open up and let the others sit within them

parts.note: so really is so tired, in the intensifying sense
left is L, and the clue trades it in for the letter Yolanda begins with
am marks the hours before noon
an ilk is a kind or sort, as in others of that ilk

explanation.walkthrough: 'Kind' is the noun, not the adjective, and the smooth breakfast surface about generous hosts is built to keep you reading it the other way.
explanation.definitionFit: It is the plant-based white liquid vegans pour on cereal in place of dairy, a staple of the vegan shopping list.
